html:
The blistering rally in artificial intelligence took a sharp breather amid an aggressive sector rotation on Wall Street. The Nasdaq plunged 4.2% on Friday alone, fueled by a combination of a blowout jobs report, which has investors pricing in an impending Federal Reserve rate hike, and underwhelming guidance from chip giant Broadcom. However, beneath these macroeconomic headwinds lies a structural demand for capital that is fundamentally reshaping tech stock allocations: the monumental liquidity requirement for SpaceX’s upcoming Initial Public Offering (IPO).

Scheduled to open for trading on Friday, Elon Musk’s rocketry and communications giant is set to execute the largest IPO in history. At an offer price of $135 per share, SpaceX will debut with a staggering valuation of roughly $1.8 trillion. Because the company positions its primary growth engine in space-based AI data centers, representing over 90% of its projected $28.5 trillion total addressable market, it competes directly for the same investment capital currently concentrated in terrestrial mega-cap tech.

To participate in an offering of this unprecedented magnitude, institutional investors and index fund managers are being forced to aggressively liquidate existing assets to free up cash.

This urgent need for liquidity has prompted investors to trim profits from highly concentrated, high-flying semiconductor and AI server stocks such as Dell, Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, and CrowdStrike. This capital flight is further compounded by Nasdaq’s relaxation of listing rules, setting the stage for SpaceX to join the Nasdaq-100 within weeks. Consequently, index managers must proactively carve out billions in liquidity from legacy tech holdings to accommodate this massive new benchmark heavyweight.
